vignette:
Layla believed for sixty-eight years that she understood the world. It was a place where you worked hard, loved your family, and found comfort in the familiar rhythms of your neighborhood. That world shattered eight months ago. Now, at sixty-nine, she felt she knew nothing at all. The man who began appearing at the fast-food restaurant where she worked was unremarkable at first, just another customer. But then he started lingering, his eyes fixed on her as she wiped down counters or filled drink orders. Soon, he was at her bus stop in the evenings. Then, he was simply there, a silent figure across the street from the apartment she shared with her husband, Nabil. The most terrifying night, she came home to find a single, wilting rose on her doormat. As she snatched it up and fumbled with her keys, she caught the scent of his cheap, musky cologne hanging in the air and saw his silhouette retreat into the alley.

Since then, safety has become a full-time job. Sleep offers no escape; Layla wakes three or four times a night, a jolt of adrenaline pulling her from a shallow doze. She slips out of bed and begins her patrol, her bare feet silent on the worn linoleum. She checks the deadbolt on the front door, twisting the knob until her knuckles ache. She ensures the flimsy latch on the kitchen window is secure. Only after confirming every point of entry is sealed does a temporary, fragile sense of calm allow her to return to bed, where she lies awake, listening. During the day, the vigilance follows her to work. Behind the counter, she no longer sees customers; she sees potential threats. She finds herself scanning every face, every shift in posture or tone of voice, searching for the flicker of malice she is now certain lurks behind most smiles. She has come to believe that people cannot be trusted, that their intentions are hidden and dangerous. Her manager has spoken to her twice about her distractedness.

The memory of those weeks is a strange and fractured thing. When her husband encourages her to talk about it, the story sometimes spills out of her as a flat, emotionless list of facts. She can describe the man's jacket, the color of the rose, the exact words on the one note he left, but she feels a profound numbness as she speaks, as if recounting a scene from a television show she once saw. It is so extreme, so outside the bounds of her life experience, that it feels impossible that it could have actually happened to her. At other times, the memory ambushes her with terrifying clarity. Standing at the stove, the scent of spices in the air will suddenly be replaced by the cloying sweetness of that cologne, and she is back on her doorstep, heart hammering against her ribs, the feeling of being watched crawling over her skin. She has learned to push these thoughts away the moment they surface. To dwell on them, she is sure, would be to let them consume her entirely. She is certain she would not be able to handle it.

This constant state of alert has hollowed her out. The woman who laughed easily with her neighbors and knew the names of all her regular customers is gone. In her place is a stranger, a frightened woman who flinches at sudden noises and sees danger in every shadow. She feels she doesn't know herself anymore. She has stopped meeting her friends for coffee and makes excuses when her sister calls to invite her over. The isolation has become a protective shell, but it is also a prison. It was after Nabil found her staring at the locked front door late one night, her hand hovering over the bolt, that he finally insisted she seek help. "I don't recognize you, Layla," he had said, his voice thick with a sorrow that cut through her fear. Layla agreed, not out of hope, but out of sheer exhaustion. She is terrified of being asked to unlock the memories she has fought so hard to contain, but a flicker of the woman she used to be desperately wants to feel at home in her own life again.
